strengths: Novel identification and characterization of Imitation Shock phenomenon with convincing universality across diverse settings (teachers, datasets, scales, domains)
Rigorous mechanistic analysis using token-level investigations, checkpoint-wise interventions, and loss-transfer matrices demonstrating functional incompatibility between anchor and reasoning tokens
Comprehensive experimental coverage including ablations against static baselines (Table 12), OOD reasoning evaluation, forgetting mitigation, and cross-model transferability studies
Strong empirical results: Qwen3-8B surpasses DeepSeek-R1 on AIME with only 200 examples; Qwen3-32B approaches 235B performance; SOTA for 16B no-think models
Clear, well-motivated presentation with logical progression from phenomenon identification through mechanistic analysis to practical solution
Thorough supplementary analysis (Appendices A-H) addressing potential confounds, gradient geometry, static signal insufficiency, and detailed experimental setups
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core method is straightforward token masking; the primary contribution is identifying what to mask rather than developing new techniques, with token prioritization well-established in related domains

Scope limited to small-data efficient distillation (primarily 200 examples); single 65K-example experiment doesn't thoroughly evaluate T3S at scale; applicability to large-scale modern distillation unclear

Mechanism underspecified: while anchor-token suppression of other tokens is demonstrated, the underlying cause is not fully explained; why does suppression weaken after anchor stabilization; is this gradient scaling, parameter interference, or something else

Practical limitations: (1) requires training accuracy verifier at each checkpoint, with no quantified computational overhead or sensitivity to verifier noise; (2) dLLM extension uses indirect AR selector proxy; (3) bottleneck definition based on training (not validation) accuracy lacks justification

Statistical rigor gaps: results averaged over 16 runs but confidence intervals inconsistently reported; some improvements modest (2-3 points); trajectory plots lack error bars; no analysis of statistical significance

Limited analysis of failure modes and boundary conditions: method works consistently across all tested settings but lacks discussion of scenarios where T3S would not help or what student-teacher properties determine Imitation Shock severity
dLLM extension less convincing: union masking (Eq. 10) is less principled than AR masking; requires external AR selector creating indirection; smaller improvements relative to AR baseline

Incomplete methodological comparisons: no comparison to other distillation methods addressing similar issues; RRT introduced by this paper not existing baseline; related token-prioritization work (Wang et al. 2025, Lin et al. 2024b) not compared experimentally
Reproducibility constraints: relies on restricted-access models (Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1); many details in appendices; design choices (τ=0.2) somewhat arbitrary; no code availability mentioned
Threshold sensitivity incompletely explored: τ=0.2 for dLLMs shows performance cliff but limited sensitivity analysis range; Table 7 suggests sharp transitions but underlying causes not explained

strengths: Identifies a novel and pervasive empirical phenomenon (Imitation Shock) with strong evidence across multiple settings, teachers, datasets, and domains
Provides extensive mechanistic investigation including token-level dynamics, interventions, and loss-transfer analysis that constrains possible explanations
Demonstrates consistent practical improvements across AR and dLLM settings with only hundreds of training examples and simple-to-implement masking approach
Includes thoughtful ablations and baselines (static confidence comparisons, -T3S inversion) that strengthen claims about trajectory-aware targeting
Well-executed experimental work with comprehensive appendices examining cross-model transferability, universality across settings, and robustness to design choices
weaknesses: Mechanistic understanding remains shallow: why exactly do early-learned anchor tokens suppress other tokens? The intervention shows correlation but not underlying mechanism (gradient interference, feature saturation, parameter coupling unclear)

Scope severely limited: only ≤200 example distillation regime tested, primarily math reasoning benchmarks, gains on OOD reasoning and retention much smaller (Tables 10-11), unclear if phenomena scale to realistic distillation settings or larger models

Method entirely depends on correctly identifying Imitation Bottleneck via training accuracy, requiring gold labels/verifiers; no sensitivity analysis on bottleneck detection errors and no guidance for practitioners

Weak theoretical foundation: no formal analysis explaining when/why Imitation Shock occurs, no characterization of conditions under which method should work, treats phenomenon as empirical observation without deeper understanding

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only compares to vanilla SFT, not recent distillation methods (DPO, RLFT, iterative approaches); -T3S ablation showing collapse doesn't prove T3S selects correct partition since aggressive masking generally hurts

Limited investigation of when method fails: all experiments show T3S helps, raising suspicions; no analysis of settings where Imitation Shock doesn't occur or where masking could hurt

Bottleneck definition using Δc_t > 0 arbitrary: why is bottleneck the right reference point versus other checkpoints? Definition somewhat circular (anchors defined by confidence increase, then shown to suppress others)
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned, dependence on specific proprietary models (Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1), many details relegated to appendices

strengths: Identifies and characterizes Imitation Shock, a previously undocumented failure mode in continual distillation, with compelling evidence across diverse settings (teachers, datasets, models, domains)

Provides rigorous mechanistic analysis combining token-level dynamics, recovering-residual transfer, checkpoint-wise intervention, and loss-transfer matrices that convincingly demonstrate anchor-token suppression
Achieves impressive practical results: Qwen3-8B surpasses DeepSeek-R1 teacher with 200 examples; Qwen3-32B approaches Qwen3-235B performance; consistent OOD gains and reduced catastrophic forgetting
Thorough experimental validation with multiple baselines, ablations (especially -T3S showing collapse), sensitivity analyses, and comprehensive appendices addressing related design choices
Extends method successfully to both AR and dLLM settings, demonstrating generality beyond autoregressive paradigm
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective figures that communicate the phenomenon and mechanism; logical progression from observation to analysis to solution
Demonstrates that trajectory-based token selection outperforms static confidence-based heuristics through controlled experiments (Appendices F-G)
weaknesses: Mechanistic explanation incomplete: while paper shows anchor tokens suppress reasoning tokens (causally via Figure 5), it does not explain *why* this suppression occurs—lacks optimization dynamics or loss landscape perspective on the interaction

Small-scale experimental setup: results on 8B-32B models with ~200 examples; scalability to modern large-scale settings (100B+ models, 10K+ example training) is unexplored

strengths: Well-characterized and reproducible phenomenon: Imitation Shock is thoroughly documented across teachers, datasets, scales, student models, and domains (Figures 1-2), establishing universality with convincing evidence.

Comprehensive mechanistic analysis: Token-level bifurcation (Figure 4), checkpoint-wise causal interventions (Figure 5), gradient dynamics (Figure 6), and loss-transfer asymmetries (Table 6) together provide strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

Strong empirical results across diverse settings: Qwen3-8B surpasses DeepSeek-R1 with 200 examples, Qwen3-32B approaches 235B performance, LLaDA-2.0-Mini achieves state-of-the-art for 16B no-think models, with consistent improvements across datasets/teachers/domains.

Rigorous experimental validation: The -T3S ablation dramatically fails, static confidence baselines are shown insufficient (Appendix K), robustness is demonstrated across scaling (Table 14), sensitivity analysis (Table 8), and cross-family transfer (Appendix C).

Practical and simple method: T3S requires no architectural changes, works with OOD teachers, extends to diffusion models, and has a simple heuristic variant (T3S-simple) that nearly matches the full method.

Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-organized narrative from observation to solution, informative visualizations, comprehensive appendices with detailed experimental setup (Appendix I) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding of root cause: The paper describes how confidence bifurcates but not why, remaining largely phenomenological. No fundamental optimization principle explains why Imitation-Anchor Tokens consistently dominate despite being less reasoning-relevant.

Dependence on training accuracy for bottleneck identification: Requires gold answers or automatic verifier, limiting applicability. The near-equivalence of T3S-simple (fixed step 10) suggests the bottleneck signal may be less critical than claimed, and robustness to noisy signals is not analyzed.

dLLM extension uses indirect AR proxy mechanism: Identifying yet-to-learn tokens via AR selector introduces external model dependency not thoroughly analyzed. Union masking (Eq. 9) appears ad-hoc, and why this approach is optimal for diffusion models is unclear.

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and generalization boundaries: All experiments focus on math/code reasoning with no discussion of when Imitation Shock might not occur, whether anchor tokens could be reasoning-critical in other domains, or applicability beyond reasoning distillation.

Extreme values in loss-transfer matrix unexplained: Table 6 shows cross-group losses increasing by up to +513%, magnitudes that warrant explanation. Unclear if 50-step training on 200 samples amplifies artificial effects or if results would hold with longer training horizons.

Statistical reporting issues: Results are averages over 16 runs without error bars, confidence intervals, or formal significance testing. Some improvements appear modest relative to unquantified variance (e.g., T3S-simple vs. T3S in Table 7).

Limited baseline comparisons: Comparisons with GKD, SWITCH, Mix Distillation are in appendices and often require tokenizer-sharing. Curriculum learning approaches and other token importance methods are underexplored despite relevance.

Incomplete semantic analysis of token patterns: Word clouds (Figure 3) are limited. Missing analysis of what semantic categories anchor vs. yet-to-learn tokens represent, token type correlations, and how anchor/other ratios vary across examples.

strengths: Identifies a real and well-documented phenomenon (Imitation Shock) with universal presence across diverse settings (teachers, datasets, scales, domains)
Thorough multi-level empirical investigation combining parameter-level, token-level, causal, and functional analyses that convincingly establishes the mechanism
Strong empirical results across multiple settings, achieving impressive performance gains with limited data (Qwen3-8B surpassing DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-32B approaching Qwen3-235B)
Simple and practical method that is straightforward to implement via token masking
Extensive experimental validation including comprehensive ablations, robustness checks, sensitivity analyses, and cross-domain/architecture evaluations
Careful methodological approach with multiple forms of evidence (RRT, loss-transfer matrix, gradient analysis, one-step interventions)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding of why anchor tokens dominate early optimization; the paper documents phenomena and shows evidence of coupling but lacks principled explanation of the underlying mechanism

Methodological circularity: token identification requires running training first; bottleneck identification is retrospective; practical overhead of computing confidence at every checkpoint is underestimated

Modest methodological novelty: masking easy/early-learned tokens resembles curriculum learning and existing token-weighting approaches; distinction from static heuristics is primarily an engineering contribution

Narrow experimental scope: heavy focus on Qwen3-8B/32B models with limited architectural diversity; primary domain is mathematical reasoning (AIME); unclear generalization to other distillation settings, models, or domains

Inadequate statistical reporting: no error bars or confidence intervals despite 16-run averaging; performance differences (especially between T3S and RRT) appear modest and may not be significant given unknown variance

Practical constraints not fully acknowledged: method requires access to training accuracy/verifiers for bottleneck identification; bottleneck selection remains somewhat ad-hoc despite robustness claims in Table 8
dLLM extension (Section 4.3) feels underdeveloped, using an AR selector as proxy rather than direct measurement, making the mechanism less transparent
Incomplete ablations: -T3S ablation is valuable but broader sensitivity analysis (e.g., to ∆ct threshold) and failure mode characterization are missing
Missing comparisons to related curriculum learning and token-selection methods beyond static confidence baselines; limited discussion of interaction with other techniques (DPO, RL)
Dense presentation with multiple concepts introduced rapidly; key insights about the solution's relationship to the phenomenon could be made more explicit earlier

strengths: Novel and systematically validated empirical phenomenon: Imitation Shock is discovered across diverse settings (teachers, datasets, scales, models, domains) with convincing visualization and measurement

Strong mechanistic understanding through multiple evidence types: token confidence bifurcation, causal one-step interventions, gradient dynamics analysis (17× norm ratios, -0.4 to -0.5 cosine similarity), and loss-transfer asymmetries (Table 6) demonstrating functional incompatibility

Practical and highly effective method: simple token masking achieving remarkable results (Qwen3-8B surpasses DeepSeek-R1 on AIME25 with 200 examples; Qwen3-32B approaches Qwen3-235B performance; LLaDA-2.0-Mini achieves 16B SOTA)

Comprehensive experimental validation: robustness to bottleneck selection (fixed step 10 works well despite variation), clear separation from static confidence heuristics, extensive ablations (RRT, -T3S), OOD evaluation (Table 12), forgetting mitigation (Table 13), and cross-model transferability analysis
Successful extension to both AR and dLLM paradigms with principled adaptations (union masking for diffusion), demonstrating method generality beyond autoregressive models
Clear presentation with thorough reproducibility details: well-motivated narrative, extensive appendices, detailed experimental setup, and transparent robustness analysis enabling future work
weaknesses: Limited theoretical foundation: no formal analysis of why Imitation Shock emerges, why it occurs despite strong student reasoning ability, or what properties of distillation objectives cause anchor-induced suppression—mechanistic understanding is empirically grounded but lacks theoretical justification

Narrow evaluation scope: primary evaluation heavily weighted toward mathematical reasoning (AIME24/25), with OOD evaluation showing smaller gains (Table 12), code reasoning in single experiment, and generalization to non-reasoning tasks (writing, translation, QA) unclear

Practical limitations inadequately addressed: requires gold answers/training accuracy for bottleneck identification (limiting applicability), dLLM extension requires external AR selector model, computational overhead of checkpoint-wise evaluation not quantified, and varying bottleneck locations despite T3S-simple using fixed step 10

Incomplete baseline comparisons: limited evaluation against existing distillation methods (only GKD, SWITCH, Mix Distillation in H.2), no comparison with other trajectory-aware or token-priority approaches, RRT baseline is oracle-based requiring bottleneck search, and recent RL-based distillation methods not compared

dLLM extension lacks theoretical grounding: using AR-defined yet-to-learn tokens as proxy for diffusion-model learning difficulties is pragmatic but unmotivated; union masking (Eq. 9) fundamentally differs from AR masking (Eq. 5) with unclear principle transfer; improvements are smaller than AR setting

Experimental design gaps: all main experiments use 50 training steps (long-training behavior unclear), no error bars or significance tests in main tables, hyperparameter sensitivity (learning rate, batch size) unexplored, and scaling results (Table 14) show diminishing gains at 100K scale with unclear limiting factors

Technical choices lack justification: alternative confidence metrics unexplored, crude anchor definition A(x,y) = {t | Δc_t > 0} without threshold exploration, bottleneck selection criteria (lowest accuracy) not compared with alternatives, and τ = 0.2 for dLLM appears somewhat arbitrary
